beats.say: Your pod restarts, and every file it wrote is gone.
A container starts with a clean disk each time. That is by design.
beats.label: Ephemeral
beats.head: A clean disk on every start

beats.say: This port has three steps: volumes, claims, and StatefulSets.
beats.label: Port 5 · Storage

beats.say: First: storage that outlives a crash.
A volume belongs to the pod, not to the container. A crash does not clear it.
beats.label: Volume
beats.head: It belongs to the pod

beats.say: But the simplest volume is deleted with the pod. It is scratch space.
beats.label: emptyDir
beats.head: Gone when the pod is gone

check.prompt: Your pod is deleted. Its data was on a PersistentVolumeClaim. Where is the data?
check.why: A claim outlives the pod. A new pod that mounts the same claim reads the same data.

beats.say: Second: storage that outlives the pod.
Your app asks for a size. It does not name a disk.
beats.label: Claim
beats.head: Ask for size, not for a disk

beats.say: A storage class makes the disk. The claim binds to it and stays.
beats.label: Dynamic provisioning
beats.head: The class makes the disk

check.prompt: Pod pg-1 of a StatefulSet is replaced. What does the new pod get?
options: A random name and a new disk
The name pg-1 and the same disk
check.why: A StatefulSet gives each replica a stable name and its own claim.

beats.say: Third: a database needs a name.
A StatefulSet gives each pod a fixed name, and its own disk.
beats.label: StatefulSet
beats.head: A fixed name and its own disk

beats.say: Pods start in order. And when you delete the set, the disks stay.
beats.label: Careful
beats.head: Delete the set: disks stay

beats.say: Containers forget. Claims remember. StatefulSets give a name and a disk.
beats.label: Storage

beats.say: Now start the first lesson below.
